ta-l1d21q2-d1e97.summary: Transitional paragraph introducing exclusive words added on the side of the predicate, in two articles: whether 'the Trinity is the only God' (Trinitas est solus Deus) is true, and whether 'the Father is the only God' is true.

ta-l1d21q2-d1e109.summary: First argument that 'the Trinity is the only God' is false. 'Solus', like 'omnis', is a disposition of the subject, and 'omnis' is incongruously added to a predicate.
claims: Solus, like omnis, qualifies the subject.

ta-l1d21q2-d1e112.summary: Second argument. Transposed names and verbs signify the same (the Philosopher), so if 'the Trinity is the only God' (solus Deus) is true, so is 'the Trinity is God alone' (Deus solus).
claims: Transposition does not change meaning.

ta-l1d21q2-d1e115.summary: Third argument. 'Solus' is syncategorematic and implies a negation, which must precede a composition or something negated; in 'the Father is the only God' nothing follows it, so the locution is false or incongruous.
claims: Negation must precede what it negates.

ta-l1d21q2-d1e119.summary: Fourth argument. Predicate terms are taken formally, and solitude does not fit a form, which is of itself communicable, so 'solus' should not be placed in the predicate.
claims: Predicates are taken formally, and forms are communicable.

ta-l1d21q2-d1e125.summary: Thomas's determination. 'Solus' and 'tantum' differ: 'tantum', an adverb (like 'solum'), determines the verb's act, and since the verb joins predicate to subject and relates to both, these adverbs can fittingly be joined to subject or predicate. 'Solus', a noun depriving of companionship, determines that with which there can be companionship, which is that to which something belongs, signified as subject, so it is properly a disposition of the subject. On this basis some say 'the Trinity is the only God' is improper: taken properly, 'solus' is not added to a predicate, and taken as 'tantum' it is superfluous with a substantial predicate ('Socrates is only a man'), since an exclusive word excludes only what is foreign in nature, which the substantial predicate already excludes; 'the Trinity is only God' would be superfluous unless 'one' or some accidental term were added to exclude plurality. They say Augustine meant not that 'solus Deus' is predicated of the Trinity but that 'solus Deus' supposits for the Trinity and not for the Father or the Son. Thomas thinks this unnecessary. Although 'solus' disposes a subject, it need not always be added to the subject, since what is in the predicate can be signified as the supposit of some nature or property, from which companionship can be removed ('Socrates is the only man sitting'). Moreover, 'God' is predicated of the three persons differently from 'man' of Socrates and Plato. 'Man' predicates only the common human nature, which in itself is not subsistent, so it predicates an inhering nature as inhering and cannot take 'solus', since a common nature does not itself have companionship but companionship is had in it. 'God' predicates the divine nature of the three persons, which is subsistent in itself even without considering the distinction of persons. Though it predicates the divine nature as nature, what it predicates is something subsistent, so it can have companionship in it, as signified as that in which, and of it, as signified as what is. So 'solus' can be added to it in the predicate as to a subsistent thing, excluding everything foreign from sharing the predicate's form: 'the Trinity is that God other than whom no other is God'. Its truth is more explicit with an addition: 'the Trinity is the only true God' or 'the only one God'.
claims: 'Solus' is properly a disposition of the subject, but can be added to a predicate signifying a subsistent.
'Deus', unlike 'homo', predicates a subsistent nature, so 'the Trinity is the only God' is true.
'The Trinity is the only true God' expresses the truth more explicitly.

ta-l1d21q2-d1e128.summary: Reply to the first argument. 'Omnis' and 'solus' dispose a subject differently. 'Omnis', by distribution, implies a division of the subject and multiplication by what it contains, so it is incongruous with terms that have no multitude of supposits, like singular terms. For this reason it cannot be in the predicate, since a predicate is taken formally and supposits are united, not distinguished, in a common form. 'Solus' implies no division but only removes companionship regarding something belonging to a subsistent, so it can fittingly be added when a subsistent thing is predicated, as with 'God'.
claims: 'Omnis' distributes and so cannot be in the predicate; 'solus' only removes companionship and can modify a subsistent predicate.

ta-l1d21q2-d1e131.summary: Reply to the second argument. When 'solus' follows its noun in the predicate, it always implies solitude, since then companionship is excluded simply and not with respect to something determinate, nothing following it. So although 'the Trinity is the only God' is granted, 'the Trinity is God alone' is not, properly speaking, because of the implied negation. 'Solus' is not like 'albus', since a negation placed after a term differs from one placed before it.
claims: 'Deus solus' (postposed) implies solitude; 'solus Deus' (preposed) does not.

ta-l1d21q2-d1e134.summary: Reply to the third argument. In 'the Trinity is the only God' or 'the only true God' a twofold composition is understood: the principal one implied by the verb, and another in 'God' as signifying one having deity. By reason of the second, exclusion can be made, excluding something from sharing the form of the predicate that belongs to the subsistent thing predicated.
claims: 'Deus' contains an implicit composition (habens deitatem) that grounds the exclusion.

ta-l1d21q2-d1e138.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. 'God' predicates the divine nature not only as form, like other substantial predicates, signified as that by which it is, but as a subsistent thing, signified as that which is, and so 'solus' can be added to it. 'God' is partly like a common term and partly like a singular term (Dist. 19).
claims: 'Deus' predicates the divine nature as subsistent (quod est), not merely as form (quo est).

ta-l1d21q2-d1e150.summary: First argument that the Father is the only God. Whatever is predicated of the three persons together is an essential predicate, and 'only God' is such, since the Trinity is the only God. Every essential predicate can be said of the Father, so the Father is the only God.
claims: What is said of the three together is essential.

ta-l1d21q2-d1e153.summary: Second argument. The Father is God and is nothing other than God, so he is the only God.
claims: The Father is nothing other than God.

ta-l1d21q2-d1e156.summary: Third argument. There is only one God, and the God other than whom there is no God is the Father, so the Father is the one only God.
claims: The Father is the God other than whom there is no God.

ta-l1d21q2-d1e163.summary: Thomas's determination. In 'the Father is the only God', 'solus', though in the predicate, can be understood on the side of the subject, as 'is a white man' can mean 'a man is white', and then it is judged like 'the Father alone is God'. If it is understood on the side of the predicate, 'solus' can be taken as 'tantum', and then it is true and not superfluous: the Son, though God, is not only God, being also man, which cannot be said of the Father, though the Father could have assumed a human nature. But that is not the sense here. If 'solus' is taken properly, the locution is proper because 'God' predicates the divine nature not only as form but as subsistent. Then it is twofold. If 'solus' excludes everything other (aliud) than the Father from sharing the predicate's form, it is true, since Son and Spirit are not another thing from the Father's supposit. If it excludes another (alius, masculine), it is false. In that sense 'the Trinity is the only God' is still true: when 'God' is predicated of the Trinity it predicates the supposit of the whole Trinity, so even with exclusion by another supposit it is true, since no supposit outside the Trinity, and no other nature, is God. But in 'the Father is God', 'God' predicates the Father's supposit, so exclusion of what is another supposit from the Father makes it false, and in this sense it is denied, while exclusion of what is other in nature from the Father makes it true.
claims: 'The Father is the only God' is true if 'solus' means 'tantum' (the Father is not also man) or excludes another nature; false if it excludes another supposit.
'The Trinity is the only God' is true even excluding other supposits, since 'Deus' then stands for the whole Trinity.

ta-l1d21q2-d1e166.summary: Reply to the first argument. As 'solus' excludes a foreign supposit and not only a foreign nature, the implicit negation extends further in 'the Father is the only God' than in 'the Trinity is the only God', since in the former the supposits of Son and Spirit are also excluded. So in that sense 'the Father is the only God' is false though 'the Trinity is the only God' is true. This is not because of the essential predicate but because of the negation excluding that supposit.
claims: The implicit negation excludes more supposits with 'the Father' as subject than with 'the Trinity'.

ta-l1d21q2-d1e169.summary: Reply to the second argument. If 'solus' is taken properly, that is not its exponent; it would be its exponent if 'solus' meant 'tantum', in which sense it was granted.
claims: 'Nothing other than God' expounds 'tantum', not 'solus'.

ta-l1d21q2-d1e172.summary: Reply to the third argument. Taking 'solus' properly, the argument does not prove that the Father is the only God but rather that God alone is Father, which was granted in some sense. The premise 'the Father is that God other than whom there is no other' is ambiguous. If the relative 'whom' refers to the Father's distinct supposit, meaning 'other than the Father there is no other', it is true if understood as 'no other God', since the Son is not another God from the Father, and false if 'no other who is God', since the Son is another than the Father and is God. If the relative refers to the supposit indistinctly, as 'God' supposits in 'God is one', it is true in every sense. So the conclusion follows only in the sense in which the proposition was granted.
claims: The premise is true or false depending on whether the relative refers to the distinct supposit of the Father or to the supposit indistinctly.

ta-l1d21q2-d1e181.summary: An expositio textus on 'No one knows the Father but the Son' (Matt. 11:27). Augustine seems to expound it badly, since 'no one' (nemo) means 'no man', which does not include the Father or the Spirit, of whom 'man' is not predicated, so his addition that Father and Spirit are not thereby separated seems unfitting. Some say 'nisi' here is adversative, not exceptive: no mere human knows the Father with comprehension, but only the Son. Better: 'nemo' has something from its proper signification and something from usage. By signification it means 'no human', which does not include the Father or Spirit. But because a human is human by having intellect, and nothing having intellect is evident to our senses except humans, by usage 'nemo' distributes over every intellectual nature, so one can descend under it to divine, angelic, and human persons.
claims: 'Nemo' by usage distributes over every intellectual nature, including divine persons.

ta-l1d21q2-Dd1e92.summary: The Prooemium of Question 2 introduces exclusive words on the side of the predicate: 'the Trinity is the only God' and 'the Father is the only God'.

ta-l1d21q2-Dd1e101.summary: Article 1 asks whether 'the Trinity is the only God' is true. Thomas distinguishes adverbial 'tantum', which can qualify either term, from nominal 'solus', properly a disposition of the subject, and rejects the view that 'solus Deus' only supposits for the Trinity. Because 'Deus', unlike 'homo', predicates a subsistent nature, 'solus' can be added to it in the predicate, so 'the Trinity is the only (true) God' is true. Postposed 'Deus solus' implies solitude, and 'omnis', unlike 'solus', distributes and so cannot be in the predicate.
claims: 'The Trinity is the only God' is true because 'Deus' predicates a subsistent.
'Deus solus' implies solitude; 'solus Deus' does not.

ta-l1d21q2-Dd1e142.summary: Article 2 asks whether 'the Father is the only God' is true. It is true if 'solus' means 'tantum', since the Father, unlike the Son, is not also man, or if it excludes what is other in nature. It is false if it excludes another supposit, since in it 'Deus' stands for the Father's supposit, whereas in 'the Trinity is the only God' it stands for the whole Trinity. The arguments for it depend on ambiguous relative reference or on exponents of 'tantum'.
claims: 'The Father is the only God' is false in the sense excluding other supposits, true in other senses.

ta-l1d21q2-Dd1e176.summary: The Expositio textus of Distinction 21 explains Augustine's reading of 'no one knows the Father but the Son', showing that 'nemo' by usage distributes over every intellectual nature.
claims: 'Nemo' by usage covers every intellectual nature.

ta-l1d21q2.summary: Quaestio 2 of Book I, Distinction 21 examines exclusive words on the side of the predicate. Article 1 holds that 'the Trinity is the only God' is true. 'Solus', though properly a disposition of the subject, can be added to the predicate 'Deus', since 'Deus', unlike 'homo', predicates a subsistent nature, while postposed 'Deus solus' would imply solitude. Article 2 holds that 'the Father is the only God' is false if 'solus' excludes other supposits, since there 'Deus' stands for the Father's supposit. It is true if 'solus' means 'tantum' or excludes another nature. The Expositio explains the extended use of 'nemo' for every intellectual nature.
claims: 'The Trinity is the only God' is true; 'the Father is the only God' is false when excluding other persons.
'Deus' predicates a subsistent nature, allowing 'solus' in the predicate.
